articles.title: World Series 2026: Sal Frelick delivers 'electric' home run to tie Game 2 as Brewers rally for yet another comeback victory
articles.summary: "Our offense is built to kind of chip away and wear on pitchers, which I think can be good when you're trying to come back," the Brewers' right fielder said.
articles.body:
MILWAUKEE — In the days leading up to the 2026 World Series, Sal Frelick wasn't trying to do much out of the ordinary. With some extra days off after the Brewers' sweep of the Dodgers in the NLCS, he had time to do something he enjoys throughout the season: Go to Catholic mass.

But Brewers fever doesn't stop at the church doorsteps.

"The priest was getting into it a little bit, [talking about] having a watch party at the church. I was sitting in the back pew, like, 'This is cool,'" Frelick said before the World Series. "We're kind of getting amped in Sunday mass."

After hitting one of the biggest home runs in Brewers' postseason history on Saturday to help lead the Brewers to a 5-4 victory in Game 2 , Frelick might have just become Milwaukee's most popular parishioner.

"We've got an early flight, so I've got to check the mass times," Frelick said Saturday night with a smile. "I hope they all watched tonight and can bring them some joy, along with the rest of the city."

Going into Frelick's sixth-inning at-bat, momentum had been building for the Brewers in what was then a 4-3 ballgame. They had fallen behind the Rays 4-0 in the first inning, but Milwaukee was chipping away against Tampa ace Drew Rasmussen. Once Rasmussen exited the game in the fourth inning, the Brewers continued their charge against the Rays' bullpen.

Leading off the sixth against southpaw Ian Seymour, Frelick was looking to do something he has done a lot this postseason: get on base. The stage was set between familiar foes, as the Brewers' right fielder had faced the Rays' left-hander in college, when he played for Boston College and Seymour was at Virginia Tech.

The at-bat Saturday mirrored many the Brewers have worked this postseason, as Frelick had to battle the Rays' southpaw. Seeing a mix of two-seam and four-seam fastballs, he spoiled them, looking for a pitch he could put in play.

"He's pretty much a sinker guy. Was fouling them off. Missed a few good ones," Frelick said afterward. "And then late in the at-bat, he started throwing four-seams and kind of caught me by surprise. Was able to spoil a few of those and was just really hoping, because I had seen the sinker earlier, that he would maybe leave one over the plate — and yeah, he did."

On the ninth pitch of the at-bat, the biggest swing of Frelick's life hammered Seymour's 3-2 four-seamer to straightaway center field and sent the American Family Field crowd of 43,245 into an uproar.

As Tampa Bay center fielder Jonny DeLuca sprinted toward the wall, every person in the Brewers' dugout and every fan in the ballpark rose to their feet. And as the 408-foot shot sailed over the wall, tying the game at 4, pandemonium ensued in Milwaukee.

"It's great, sort of this blackout feeling," Frelick said.

"I almost started crying in the dugout," first baseman Jake Bauers said. "That's such an awesome moment for Sal. Such an awesome moment for the team. That guy means so much to us. To see him have an at-bat like that and hit the homer, it was an emotional moment."

Frelick isn't known for his power. He hit four home runs in the regular season, and this was just his second homer of the year off a left-handed pitcher. But whenever the Brewers have needed some pop this postseason, they've found it; they lead all playoff teams in homers.

"He's just the ultimate competitor, winner. He's got the it-factor," Brewers manager Pat Murphy said.

One inning later, shortstop Cooper Pratt hit an RBI single that gave the Brewers a 5-4 lead that held for a Game 2 victory and a commanding 2-0 World Series lead.

"It seems like we've had a lot of experience with it in the postseason," Frelick said of his team coming back. "Down early almost every game so far … Our offense is built to kind of chip away and wear on pitchers, which I think can be good when you're trying to come back."

Frelick is putting together arguably the best stretch of his career. The right fielder, who finished Game 2 2-for-4 with a homer, is hitting .273 with a .370 on-base percentage in October. He actually came within a few feet of his second homer of the game in the seventh inning, and while a two-homer game might have been nice, that would've surprised even Frelick.

"I've never hit a homer that I thought was gone," he said with a smile.

Before Frelick's blast, it had been 16,075 days since a Milwaukee Brewer hit a home run in the World Series, and it's unlikely that anyone would've picked Frelick to end that drought. But his doing so provided the next chapter in the comeback story the Brewers have gotten so good at writing.

As they've made their way to 9-1 this postseason, it's been a different hero almost every night. In Game 2, it was Frelick's turn to deliver.

"My favorite swing of the year, and it's not even close," left-hander Aaron Ashby said. "That was electric. This team wouldn't be what this team is without that guy."

articles.title: Latest MLB Trade Rumors Amid 2026 World Series Final Bracket
articles.summary: The Milwaukee Brewers took a 2-0 lead over the Tampa Bay Rays in the 2026 World Series on Saturday night.
articles.body:
The Milwaukee Brewers took a 2-0 lead over the Tampa Bay Rays in the 2026 World Series on Saturday night.

While those two teams are playing for the Commissioner's Cup and a shot at baseball immortality, the rest of MLB is considering moves, including trades, to help their teams reach the pinnacle of the sport next season.

What is the latest from around the league? Find out in this collection of insider reports from some of the game's most trusted insiders.

Barry Jackson of the Miami Herald reported on what may be a busy offseason for the Marlins this winter.

He wrote, ""Though the Marlins aren't believed to be shopping (Otto) Lopez or (Xavier) Edwards, neither player is considered untouchable. If a team is willing to offer a lot in return, Miami would listen."

Lopez was among the best hitters in the game this season, leading MLB with 191 hits and delivering a .305 batting average. He was still not a power hitter by any means, with just 11 home runs and 71 RBI, but he put the ball in play and got on base, making him an attractive piece to any big-league team looking for an offensive spark.

Edwards was worth three wins above average while hitting .280, with six home runs and 52 RBI.

Both are young (28 and 27, respectively) and have plenty of upside, so it is not particularly surprising that the Marlins would listen to offers from teams that would be interested in acquiring them.

Of course, Miami was on the cusp of playoff contention at times in 2026 and could look to beef up their roster, too, instead of subtracting from it.

Jackson wrote, "The Marlins would look to add established players making in the $10 million to $15 million range through either free agency or through trades. Miami is open to trading some of their good prospects, but not their top prospects."

An organization that has proven effective at developing young talent for other teams to come in and trade for or sign in free agency, it is not surprising that they would not look to give up their best prospects in the name of a trade for a more established player or two.

Still, adding a player who can produce offensively and is not a liability on the diamond or in the outfield could be the difference between another frustrating campaign in South Beach and a trip back to the playoffs, where they have not been since 2023.

Another disappointing Guardians playoff exit reignites questions about Steven Kwan's time in Cleveland and whether it may be coming to an end.

Robert Murray of FanSided reported that a Kwan trade is back on the table following an ALCS loss.

Like Lopez in Miami, Kwan was one of the better hitters in baseball this past season, exploding out of an early-year slump and becoming one of the driving forces behind Cleveland's re-emergence in the playoff picture.

The 29-year-old hit .282, with 32 RBI, three home runs, and 10 stolen bases. His career-high on-base percentage (.382) was key to helping the Guardians perform down the stretch and return to the playoffs.

Kwan is under team control for one more season before hitting the free agency market in 2028.

While the Guardians may be keen on finding a trade partner in hopes of maximizing their returns for Kwan, the team's playoff window will inevitably close, and getting rid of a prolific hitter who can put the team in scoring position every time he heads to the plate may expedite the process.

The team has consistently gotten close to a return to the World Series for the first time since 2016. Attempting to get over the hump and do so without Kwan would make the task that much more difficult to achieve.

Especially without a guarantee of a player who can get himself or the team into scoring position as consistently and effectively as Kwan.

articles.title: MLB World Series 2026 Box Score Stat Predictions for Brewers vs. Rays Game 3
articles.summary: The Milwaukee Brewers are two games away from winning the franchise's first World Series after taking a 2-0 lead over the Tampa Bay Rays in the Fall Classic on Saturday night.
articles.body:
The Milwaukee Brewers are two games away from winning the franchise's first World Series after taking a 2-0 lead over the Tampa Bay Rays in the Fall Classic on Saturday night.

The American League champs have a chance to claw their way back into the battle for the Commissioner's Trophy as the series heads south to Florida.

Who will be key contributors for the Rays, and which Brewers could ensure the team inches one step closer to another definitive postseason sweep?

Let's take a look at these stat predictions for Game 3.

ALCS MVP Freddy Peralta makes his World Series debut on Monday night as he takes the mound for the Rays against the team he played the majority of his career with.

While the righty was dominant against Cleveland (0.75 ERA, nine strikeouts in three appearances), he did not fare well against his friends in Milwaukee, the only time he faced them this year.

During his thankfully short stint with the New York Mets, Peralta played his former team once and was beaten up. Badly. In a July 20 start against the Brewers, Peralta went 5.1 innings, gave up eight hits, seven earned runs, and two home runs. He left the game with an ERA of 11.81.

Since moving to Tampa at the deadline, he has been a vastly improved pitcher and has been a major reason for the team's relative dominance against Cleveland. Showing improved command of his stuff and benefiting from better coaching, he has the opportunity to make up for that first showdown against the Brewers.

Do not expect nearly as disastrous a start from Peralta, especially with a 7-0 record and 0.89 ERA since August.

Prediction: 6.2 IP, 6 H, 2 ER, 2 BB, 7 K

Gasser came out of nowhere, replacing Dustin May and becoming one-third of the most electric, young starting rotation in baseball.

Beginning his year in Triple A, he has made the most of the opportunities presented to him, including key performances against the San Diego Padres and Los Angeles Dodgers, each of which helped Milwaukee get over the hump and into its first World Series in four decades.

Possessing a sweeper that will confuse any batter, he has become increasingly confident with every start.

Monday, he arrives at Tropicana Field having conceded just one run in nine postseason innings, per MLB.com .

If he can resist the moment from getting too big for him and can stay focused while throwing the stuff that has earned him this opportunity, Gasser has the goods to put his team up 3-0, with a chance to win the most coveted prize in the sport.

The 22-year-old Venezuelan has lived up to lofty expectations this offseason, particularly over the last four games against the Dodgers and Rays.

In those games, he has delivered five hits, three runs, one home run, two RBI, and two stolen bases.

He has been outstanding for the Brewers and a huge part of their success.

It is difficult to forecast how he will perform against Peralta, having played the former Brewers ace just once. In two at-bats, he walked once and struck out the other.

Considering how hot he is now, though, it is difficult to imagine such a lackluster stat line Monday night in Tampa. It may not be as sparkling as some of his other performances to this point in the postseason, but Chourio will have greater success than in his first meeting with the fastball-throwing righty.

The Rays' lack of success against Milwaukee to this point is not for lack of trying on Cameinero's part.

The 23-year-old has two hits, one run, and one strikeout against the NL champs in seven at-bats.

Against the series-deciding win over Cleveland, he delivered two hits, two runs, a home run, and two RBI in three at-bats.

Heading home to Florida, with a chance to put a dent in Milwaukee's two-game lead in this World Series, expect dramatics from Caminero as he looks to help carry the Rays back from the brink.

articles.title: Jake Bauers 'Almost Started Crying' After Frelick's HR in Brewers' Win vs. Rays in World Series G2
articles.summary: Milwaukee Brewers first baseman Jake Bauers let the moment soak in as he watched Sal Frelick's game-tying home run sail over the fence in the 6th inning of Saturday's 5-4 win over the Tampa Bay Rays.
articles.body:
Milwaukee Brewers first baseman Jake Bauers let the moment soak in as he watched Sal Frelick's game-tying home run sail over the fence in the 6th inning of Saturday's 5-4 win over the Tampa Bay Rays.

"I almost started crying in the dugout," Bauers said, per ESPN's Jesse Rogers . "He means so much to us in here."

Based on his production, Frelick isn't the first name you would've picked to deal one of the biggest blows in Game 2. He had four home runs and slugged .319 during the regular season, and his power numbers haven't gone up much in the playoffs.

But Frelick stepped up to finally erase what had been Tampa Bay's 4-0 lead after the top of the first inning. He concluded a nine-pitch at-bat by slamming an Ian Seymour fastball 408 feet to center field.

Cooper Pratt's RBI single provided the go-ahead run in the seventh.

One way or another, Brewers manager Pat Murphy expected Frelick to rise to the occasion in the Fall Classic. He called the veteran outfielder an "ultimate competitor, winner" who possesses the "'it' factor."

"You think of Joe Montana (or) Larry Bird, they have the 'it' factor," Murphy said, per The Athletic's Tyler Kepner . "I'm not saying he's at that level of talent or has been in a position to do those things, but he has that 'it' factor.

"He can take a team down the field. I'm sure when you're a man down in hockey, he can prevent guys from scoring. He just has that grit, he has that belief system, like, 'I'm going to get this done, and you're not going to deny me.'"

The fine margins of the World Series mean otherwise unheralded players often write their names into MLB lore.

Los Angeles Dodgers ace Yoshinobu Yamamoto took home MVP in the 2025 World Series, but Miguel Rojas and Andy Pages were equally instrumental in the team's Game 7 victory. Two years ago, Teoscar Hernández and Tommy Edman did some heavy lifting for the star-studded offense.

Should Milwaukee go on to lift its first title, Frelick's home run will be replayed often by the team's fans, and he may never have to pay for a drink in Wisconsin ever again.

articles.title: Junior Caminero Has 'Already Forgotten' Rays' 2 Losses to Brewers in MLB World Series
articles.summary: The Tampa Bay Rays have no choice but to move on after losing the first two games of the World Series to the Milwaukee Brewers, and Junior Caminero is doing just that.
articles.body:
The Tampa Bay Rays have no choice but to move on after losing the first two games of the World Series to the Milwaukee Brewers, and Junior Caminero is doing just that.

"I've already forgotten about these last two days," he said following Saturday's 5-4 loss, per Ken Rosenthal of The Athletic. "The series in my mind starts Monday."

It seemed like the Rays were going to earn the split in Milwaukee when they jumped out to a 4-0 lead in the first inning behind RBI singles from Chandler Simpson and Caminero as well as a two-run homer from Liam Hicks.

However, the visitors didn't score another run the rest of the game.

That they struggled with the Milwaukee bullpen comes as no surprise. Rosenthal noted Brewers relief pitchers have allowed just one run in 10 innings in this series compared to the three runs in 7.1 innings the Tampa Bay bullpen has allowed.

It is more of the same from the group that features Aaron Ashby and Abner Uribe, which also controlled the National League Championship Series sweep over the Los Angeles Dodgers.

The sixth inning didn't help, either, as the Rays made a number of mistakes.

Hicks was thrown out at home on a two-out single by Victor Mesa Jr. in the top of the frame before Sal Frelick tied the game with a homer in the bottom of the inning. What's more, Rays left fielder Chandler Simpson didn't catch a fly ball from Christian Yelich, although it was not ruled an error.

Caminero started yelling in the dugout after the inning and explained he was "trying to help the team, get our heads up. Just trying to create some energy and get some life back into us," per Rosenthal.

"We had to get outs. At that moment, we weren't doing our job," he continued. "Against Milwaukee, if you give up outs, they're going to use that against you, and that's what happened. I was trying to (convey) the message, we've got to get outs."

Perhaps things will go better for the Rays when the series shifts home. After all, Caminero is already putting the road games behind him.

articles.title: Inside the controversial call that ended Game 2 of the World Series
articles.summary: The Milwaukee Brewers are two wins away from the first World Series title in franchise history, and they got a little help from an incredibly close call Saturday night.
articles.body: The Milwaukee Brewers are two wins away from the first World Series title in franchise history, and they got a little help from an incredibly close call Saturday night. With the Brewers leading 5-4 in the top of the ninth, the Rays had a runner on third with two outs and designated hitter Yandy Díaz at the plate. On a 3-2 pitch that would have been Ball 4, Díaz tried to check his swing on a curveball from Aaron Ashby. Home plate umpire Jim Wolf initially ruled that Díaz hadn’t swung, which would have sent him to first base. But Milwaukee catcher William Contreras appealed to the first base umpire, who ruled that Díaz had gone around. The strikeout ended the game. Here’s how the swing looked in real time: And here’s how it looked on replay: “In the moment, yeah, I disagreed. But the umpire said it was a swing and it is what it is,” Díaz said after the game. “I didn’t go look at it, but from my vantage point, it did look like that he swung,” Tampa Bay manager Kevin Cash said. The postgame crew on the Fox broadcast seemed split over the swing as well. What exactly is a check swing? It’s a great question, and one that MLB’s rulebook doesn’t answer. According to MLB.com, “there is no definition for ‘check swing’ in the official baseball rules. The closest thing comes in the definition of terms where the first example of a strike is a pitch that ‘is struck at by the batter.’” That leaves it to the umpires’ discretion when a pitch is considered to be “struck at.” Colloquially, a batter has to break an imaginary plane for a check swing to be considered a full one. What exactly is that plane? Again, there’s no official rule. As with obscenity in Jacobellis v. Ohio, umpires typically know it when they see it. Why didn’t the Rays challenge the call? Much to the delight of fans, MLB introduced the automated ball-strike (ABS) system this season, allowing players to challenge, as the name suggests, balls and strikes. ABS came on top of the expanded replay review rules instituted in 2014, which granted managers at least one challenge per game on calls such as force plays, tag plays and even fan interference. Unfortunately for Tampa Bay, check swings aren’t on the list of reviewable plays, so the Rays couldn’t ask for a review of the play in Game 2. “We got ABS for the first time this year, getting the balls and strikes right. We need to get a system that can get [check swings] right,” Fox play-by-play announcer Joe Davis said during a replay of Díaz’s swing. Will this happen again? Given all the technology MLB has at its disposal, it’s hard to believe the league and players union will let a situation like Game 2’s happen again, particularly when the stakes are as high as the World Series. In 2024, MLB tested check-swing challenges in the Arizona Fall League, using the same Hawk-Eye technology used for the ABS system. In those challenges, teams were able to review if a check swing “crossed a 45-degree threshold from home plate,” according to MLB.com. The check-swing challenge has since made it to the minors, introduced to the single-A Florida State League in 2025 and the triple-A Pacific Coast League this year. In June 2025, MLB Commissioner Rob Manfred said he wanted teams to be accustomed to the ABS system before introducing the check-swing challenge to the majors. “We haven’t made a decision about the check-swing thing,” Manfred said at the time. “We do try to think sequentially about what’s coming. I think we got to get over the hump in terms of either doing ABS or not doing it before you’d get into the complication of a separate kind of challenge involved in an at-bat, right? You think about them, they’re two different systems operating at the same time. We really got to think that one through.”

articles.title: Shohei Ohtani's $700 million deal is changing the Dodgers' business, with merchandise sales soaring 10x
articles.summary: Shohei Ohtani's impact on the Los Angeles Dodgers goes far beyond his performances on the field.
articles.body: Shohei Ohtani's impact on the Los Angeles Dodgers goes far beyond his performances on the field. Since joining the team on a record-breaking $700 million contract, the Japanese superstar has helped drive merchandise sales, attract sponsors and strengthen the Dodgers' global appeal. One striking example came from Dodgers CEO Stan Kasten, who revealed that the team's store revenue had climbed from around $3,000 a day in January before Ohtani arrived to approximately $30,000 a day during his first offseason. The tenfold increase shows how one superstar can change a baseball team's business prospects.Shohei Ohtani's $700 million Dodgers contract brings a new business dimensionThe Dodgers made a major statement when they signed Ohtani to a 10-year, $700 million contract in December 2023. The deal set a new benchmark in professional sports and showed the team's belief in his value as both an elite baseball player and a global commercial figure.However, the contract's structure attracted almost as much attention as its headline value. Ohtani agreed to defer $680 million, leaving him scheduled to receive $2 million annually during the 10-year playing term. The remaining $680 million is due in annual payments of $68 million from 2034 through 2043.This arrangement gives the Dodgers greater flexibility with their payroll during Ohtani's playing years. It does not make the contract inexpensive, but it allows the club to invest in its roster while managing its immediate financial commitments.Ohtani's commercial appeal also gives the Dodgers another way to assess the deal. His performances can help the team win games, but his international profile can also attract new fans, increase merchandise demand and create opportunities for business partnerships.For the Dodgers, the long-term value of the agreement extends beyond his salary and on-field contributions. His presence has strengthened the team's connection with Japanese audiences and increased its visibility among baseball fans worldwide.Dodgers merchandise sales soar 10x after Shohei Ohtani's arrivalOne of the clearest examples of Ohtani's commercial influence came from the Dodgers' team store. Kasten discussed the change in daily sales during an appearance on Sports Business Radio.Before Ohtani arrived, the store generated around $3,000 per day in January. During Ohtani's first offseason with the team, that figure reportedly reached approximately $30,000 per day.The increase represents a tenfold jump and highlights the demand surrounding one of baseball's biggest stars. Fans wanted jerseys and other Dodgers merchandise featuring Ohtani's name, helping turn his popularity into a visible business opportunity.The figures also show why teams increasingly consider a player's marketability when evaluating major contracts. A globally recognised athlete can attract buyers who may not have previously followed the team closely. Merchandise gives those fans a direct way to show their support.Still, the numbers need context. The reported increase concerns daily revenue at the team store during a specific period. It does not mean that every Dodgers merchandise channel experienced the same increase, nor does it establish the club's total profit from Ohtani-related products.Even with those limits, the difference between $3,000 and $30,000 a day offers a compelling example of how Ohtani's arrival changed the team's retail business.Shohei Ohtani's commercial appeal extends beyond merchandise salesOhtani's financial influence reaches beyond jerseys and souvenirs. His arrival has helped raise the Dodgers' profile among Japanese fans and strengthened the team's appeal to visitors, sponsors and businesses seeking access to a wider audience.A Los Angeles Times report examined the broader commercial impact of Ohtani's first year with the club, including merchandise, ticket demand and stadium tours. Dodgers chief marketing officer Lon Rosen described the wider effect of the team's increased visibility, saying, "that means more people are thinking about the Dodgers and buying more merchandise and more tickets and more hot dogs and more everything."The comment captures an important point about sports business. A superstar can influence several sources of revenue at the same time. Fans may buy tickets to see the player, purchase merchandise, visit the stadium and follow the team more closely throughout the season.Ohtani's appeal is especially valuable because his fan base extends well beyond the United States. His success has helped the Dodgers connect with audiences in Japan, giving the franchise a stronger international presence.That wider reach can benefit the organisation in ways that are harder to measure than store sales. Greater interest can support television exposure, tourism, digital engagement and future commercial partnerships. However, each revenue stream depends on several factors, including team performance, ticket availability and broader market demand.Shohei Ohtani helps the Dodgers attract millions in sponsorship revenueOhtani's international popularity has also created opportunities for the Dodgers to work with brands looking to reach Japanese consumers.A Forbes report citing SponsorUnited estimated that the Dodgers added 12 Japan-based partners and generated $70 million in incremental sponsorship revenue associated with Ohtani in 2024. The report also estimated that visiting teams collectively received around $15 million in revenue from Japanese brand signage when hosting the Dodgers.These figures show how one player's appeal can influence commercial activity across Major League Baseball. When the Dodgers travel, their games can offer Japanese companies valuable exposure to audiences in the United States. That visibility may benefit both the home team and the league's broader commercial network.However, the sponsorship estimates should not be treated as proof that Ohtani personally generated every dollar. Sponsorship revenue depends on several factors, including the Dodgers' established brand, their audience size, negotiations with partners and the wider popularity of Major League Baseball.The figures also represent revenue rather than profit. The cost of delivering sponsorship agreements and other business expenses affects how much money a team ultimately retains.Even with these qualifications, the reported partnerships underline the commercial value of Ohtani's presence. His name and reputation can help the Dodgers appeal to businesses that might otherwise have limited interest in partnering with an American baseball team.Can Shohei Ohtani's business impact justify the Dodgers' investment?Ohtani's $700 million contract remains an enormous financial commitment. The Dodgers must balance his sporting value with the costs and risks of a long-term deal, even with most of his salary deferred.His commercial influence offers one part of the picture. The reported tenfold rise in daily team-store revenue, increased international attention and additional sponsorship opportunities suggest that his value reaches well beyond the field.However, no single figure can establish whether the contract has paid for itself. Merchandise revenue is not the same as profit, sponsorship estimates do not represent the entire financial return, and the team's overall performance affects ticket demand and fan spending.The Dodgers also benefit from Ohtani's exceptional baseball ability. His performances help drive interest in the team, while his worldwide reputation gives the franchise a commercial advantage that few players can match.The strongest conclusion is that Ohtani has become both a baseball star and a major business asset for the Dodgers. The team's reported store revenue increase from $3,000 to $30,000 a day provides a striking example of that influence, while its sponsorship activity and international reach reveal a much wider opportunity.Ohtani's contract will be judged over many years, not by one season's sales figures. For now, the evidence suggests that his arrival has helped the Dodgers strengthen their brand, expand their audience and create new commercial opportunities alongside their pursuit of championships.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: 7 Bold MLB Predictions For 2026-27 Offseason
articles.summary: Major League Baseball's offseason won't officially begin until this small-market extravaganza between the Brewers and Rays comes to an end, but it's never too early to venture some guesses at what this winter's biggest stunners will be.
articles.body:
Major League Baseball's offseason won't officially begin until this small-market extravaganza between the Brewers and Rays comes to an end, but it's never too early to venture some guesses at what this winter's biggest stunners will be.

There are always a few eyebrow-raisers that even the boldest of predictions didn't see coming.

We won't bore you with a faux "bold" prediction of Tarik Skubal signing with the Mets or Dodgers, but having him land pretty much anywhere aside from those two options would be a bold suggestion, right?

Could the A's trade away their All-Star catcher?

Will the O's trade for one year of an ace like they did a few years ago with Corbin Burnes?

Or how about the Pirates and Royals each signing one of the biggest free agents available?

We've got a total of seven bold offseason predictions here: one for each of MLB's six divisions, plus a bonus prognostication about the inevitable lockout.

AL East: Baltimore Trades for an Ace-Caliber Rental (Again)

During the 2023-24 offseason, the Baltimore Orioles traded two tantalizing prospects (Joey Ortiz and DL Hall) to the Milwaukee Brewers for one year of Corbin Burnes.

It's a trade that stings today, as Hall and Ortiz both ranked top 10 in bWAR among Brewers en route to the World Series. But in that one year in Baltimore, Burnes made 32 starts with a sub-3.00 ERA, finishing fifth in the AL Cy Young vote and giving the O's an eight-inning gem in their postseason opener. They frankly couldn't have asked for more than what they got.

There's no time like the present for them to go back to that well.

In Shane Baz, Brandon Young and Kyle Bradish (provided he makes a full recovery from sports hernia surgery), Baltimore has three certainties in its starting rotation for 2027. And the future of this rotation is bright, with Anthony Eyanson, Joseph Dzierwa and Caden Hunter all ending the year at Double-A Chesapeake as top 100 overall prospects, per MLB.com's pipeline .

For 2027, though, the rotation is looking mighty suspect.

Whether it's Baz or Bradish starting on Opening Day, let's just say Baltimore isn't projected for a top-10 spot in any sort of "Ranking the 30 Opening Day Starting Pitchers" article. There's also ample room for improvement in the combination of Trey Gibson, Cade Povich, Michael Forret and Luis De León for the No. 4 and No. 5 spots in the rotation.

Basically, Baltimore could really use one, maybe two years of an ace-caliber pitcher to hold down the fort until at least one of those top prospects is ready to shine.

Of course, the catch is they would almost certainly need to part with one of those pitching prospects—and more—to acquire a Logan Gilbert, Drew Rasmussen, Joe Ryan, Nathan Eovaldi or Sandy Alcantara, each of whom could become a free agent after the 2027 season.

They've got to do something big, though.

They didn't sign Pete Alonso for $155M so he could work on his golf game every October.

When the Kansas City Royals had their time in the sun back in 2014-15, the outfield tandem of Alex Gordon and Lorenzo Cain carried that offense. Even reserve outfielder Jarrod Dyson was a major X-factor with his speed on the basepaths.

Over the past four years, however, Kansas City's outfield situation has been all sorts of bleak.

By a considerable margin, Kyle Isbel has been their most valuable outfielder since the beginning of 2023, but only because of his defense in center. There are 203 players with at least 1,400 plate appearances over the past four seasons, and Isbel's .642 OPS ranks 200th.

Jac Caglianone arrived in a big way in 2026, though, primarily playing right field. And if the Royals could land a legitimate asset in left, they could be in business.

"Top free agent hitter" and "Kansas City Royals" don't typically go hand-in-hand. In fact, outside of re-signing Gordon on a four-year, $72M deal the winter after winning the 2015 World Series, they've never spent more than $36M on a hitter in free agency. And Arozarena (who turns 32 in February) has a projected market of 4-5 years at a bit north of $20M per year.

If they're not aggressively trying to win a World Series in 2027 or 2028, though, they might as well just embrace a rebuild now, right?

Next year will presumably be Salvador Perez's last ride, and the Royals also have a long and noteworthy list of players who could reach free agency over the next two offseasons, including Vinnie Pasquantino, Seth Lugo, Michael Wacha, Cole Ragans and Michael Massey.

While they do have Bobby Witt Jr. locked up through at least 2030, it's only going to become tougher to build a contender around him, as his cash salary climbs from $13M in 2026 to $19M next year to $30M in 2028 and $35M in both 2029 and 2030.

We don't often encourage a team to go all-in the offseason after suffering 93 losses, but now's the time for Kansas City. The Royals also went straight from 106 losses in 2023 to the postseason in 2024. Throw in what the White Sox accomplished this year and who's to say we couldn't be headed for a third case in four years of an AL Central team going from the basement to the playoffs?

AL West: Athletics Trade Away Shea Langeliers

Over the past two seasons, Shea Langeliers has been one of the five most valuable catchers in baseball.

He doesn't draw many walks, but he's batting .270 and slugging .507, trailing only Hunter Goodman in the latter department. He averaged 38 home runs per 162 games played between 2025-26.

Langeliers also made big strides as a catcher in 2026, throwing out 32 percent of would-be base-stealers after teams ran all over him in 2025.

But Langeliers has two years of arbitration eligibility remaining and an agent (Scott Boras) whose clients rarely sign extensions before reaching free agency for the first time. As a result, the A's—who have averaged 98.2 losses over the past five seasons—are probably going to put him on the trade block this offseason.

Frankly, it's so likely that the A's are at least willing to discuss a Langeliers trade that we need to make this an even bolder prediction.

So how about this: The Athletics trade Langeliers to the Yankees for a pair of young pitchers.

It won't be Cam Schlittler. I haven't completely lost my mind. But the Yankees have four more years of Will Warren, three years left on Luis Gil and a farm system in which nine of the top 10 players are pitchers, per MLB.com's pipeline . The pair of young pitchers heading to West Sacramento will come from that pool of 11 arms.

The Yankees could very much use another catcher and right-handed bat while the A's kind of need to trade their way to a competent pitching staff, as free agents are understandably reluctant to make half of their starts at the warm-weather launching pad that is Sutter Health Park.

New York will simultaneously pursue a similar trade with Colorado for Hunter Goodman, but the A's are more likely to make it happen.

Ranking Every Player in the 2026 World Series 🔢

NL East: New York Mets Replace Bo Bichette with Teruaki Sato

We're giving you a little two-for-one action on this bold prediction, with the first half of it being that Bo Bichette opts out of the latter two seasons of the 3-year, $126M contract he signed last winter.

Notably, Bichette gets a $5M buyout if he opts out, so he'd actually be leaving two years and $79M on the table. Even that might sound slightly insane after the disappointing first year that he had in Queens. At any rate, there's no realistic chance he fares better than a $39.5M AAV if he re-enters free agency.

However, in a year where Jazz Chisholm Jr. is arguably the second-most or third-most coveted free agent hitter available, a 28-year-old Bichette who has been worth more than 20 WAR in his career could probably fetch another nine-figure contract.

If he does leave, the Mets could simply hand the third-base reins to top prospect Jefferson Rojas, hoping for results similar to what Carson Benge and AJ Ewing gave them as rookies in 2026. Alternatively, they could give Brett Baty and/or Mark Vientos yet another chance to prove they can cut the mustard as an everyday third baseman.

Going after prized Japanese slugger Teruaki Sato is more their speed, though.

Whether Sato's glove is good enough for the hot corner is a concern that most teams will grapple with while trying to determine how much he's worth, but, heck, the Mets signed Bichette to be their primary third baseman when he had zero professional experience at the position.

The potential for 25 errors might not bother them if they believe Sato has the potential for 45 home runs.

The Mets also don't have a dedicated designated hitter, nor a particularly sure thing at first base, so they could try Sato out at 3B before going to a backup plan of Rojas, Baty or Vientos if it turns out they need to move the 2026 NPB Triple Crown winner to 1B or DH.

NL Central: Pittsburgh Pirates Sign Jazz Chisholm Jr.

The time has come for Pittsburgh to put its money where its mouth is.

The Pirates reportedly tried to sign both Josh Naylor and Kyle Schwarber last offseason, which would have cost more than double their previous record for money spent on a single free agent. In the end, both players re-signed with their former teams (as most expected would be the case) and the Pirates settled for short-term deals with Ryan O'Hearn, Marcell Ozuna and Gregory Soto as their "big" swings in free agency.

Thanks in large part to their one-year acquisition of Brandon Lowe, though, they turned a corner, posting a winning record for the first time since 2018 and a positive run differential for the first time since 2015—this despite Paul Skenes becoming mortal on the mound while rookie phenom Konnor Griffin and key slugger Oneil Cruz missed a combined total of 147 games.

With Lowe now headed for free agency, they need to add an infielder if they're going to chase this sudden surge of competence.

Maybe they give Lowe a qualifying offer and he returns for one year at $23.15M.

If he declines, perhaps they go the trade route again, pursuing Isaac Paredes from Houston or Ozzie Albies from Atlanta.

Or maybe *record scratch* the Pirates sign one of the best free agents available in Jazz Chisholm Jr.

It wouldn't be a long-term, nine-figure monster of a deal. Pittsburgh extended both Griffin and Bryan Reynolds for north of $100M, but they don't play that game in free agency.

But what if Dec. 1 (AKA Lockout Eve) rolls around and Chisholm—after discovering the market doesn't think he's nearly as valuable as he thinks he is—gets a phone call from a 412 area code with an offer for $30M for one season?

Come smash some home runs and pierogies on a "prove it" deal before re-entering free agency (during a normal offseason) at the age of 29?

It could be a perfect fit, and it sure would be fun to watch Cruz and Chisholm each try to get to 30 home runs and 30 stolen bases as teammates.

NL West: San Diego Padres Win Tarik Skubal Sweepstakes

Picking the Dodgers, the Mets or even the Tigers as the team that signs Tarik Skubal this winter wouldn't be bold. MLB.com's Mark Feinsand had those three, the Phillies, the Blue Jays and the Cubs among the six potential, realistic suitors who could give Skubal an historic contract.

Why aren't the Padres on that list, though, especially under new ownership?

When Steve Cohen became the Mets' principal owner in 2020, their payroll pretty much immediately skyrocketed. Same goes for when Mark Walter and the Guggenheim group bought the Dodgers back in 2012. And one kind of has to assume the group headed by Kwanza Jones and José E. Feliciano is going to be aggressively trying to win right away.

And they sure do have work to do on this pitching staff.

Assuming Michael King opts out, the Padres are going to lose six of the seven pitchers who made at least nine starts for them in 2026. They also can't possibly know what they are going to get out of Joe Musgrove and Yu Darvish in 2027, at which point the starting rotation becomes Nick Pivetta, Randy Vásquez and three big question marks.

Even though they do have a ton of money tied up in Manny Machado, Xander Bogaerts, Fernando Tatis Jr. and Jackson Merrill through 2033 and beyond, they simply have to swing big for arguably the best pitcher in the sport today.

For what it's worth, the San Francisco Giants are in a similar boat, minus the new ownership factor. That rotation gets weak in a hurry beyond Logan Webb, and they are on the hook for at least $23.5M to each of Rafael Devers, Matt Chapman and Willy Adames through at least 2030. But if they can find the room in the budget for Skubal, their outlook instantly and drastically changes.

MLB: There Will Be Baseball in 2027...But Not Initially

When the current collective bargaining agreement between Major League Baseball and the MLB Players Association expires at 11:59 p.m. ET on Dec. 1, there is going to be a lockout.

In theory, they could get a new deal done before then, but we've known for more than a year at this point that is quite unlikely to happen. The owners are pushing for a salary cap harder than at any point in the past three decades, which the players adamantly do not want. And that's merely the biggest issue on a long list of negotiations that need to take place.

As the war of words between the millionaires and billionaires plays out, though, most baseball fans are only going to care about one thing: Will the regular season go off without a hitch?

The last time a new CBA needed to be ratified during the 2021-22 offseason, that lockout lasted 99 days. But they still managed to have a full 162-game schedule, albeit slightly delayed.

If the players hold their ground and refuse to accept a salary cap, though, this one has the potential to be so much worse.

The big line in the sand on the calendar that many have cited will be in late May at the 60 games missed (per team) threshold.

Per The Athletic , if that much of the season gets canceled, that's when an additional year gets tacked onto broadcast-rights contracts, throwing quite a wrench into Rob Manfred's grand plan to gather all the streaming rights back under one umbrella after 2028. (And maybe finally getting rid of all these nonsensical blackouts that fans have had to endure/work around for years?)

If that happens, that's when this lockout would really start to hit the owners' wallets for years to come—and both sides know it.

The players are going to prepare to miss upwards of 60 games, expecting that the owners will cave before it gets that far.

My complete dart throw of a guess is that the new CBA will be ratified on April 15, there will not be a salary cap and after an abridged spring training, we'll miss 33 games per team in a season that begins on May 3. A 129-game season is far from ideal, but it would leave room for six games per league opponent and three games per interleague foe.

articles.title: Ranking Top 10 Hitters of 2026-27 MLB Free-Agent Class
articles.summary: With MLB owners expected to lock the players out when the current collective bargaining agreement expires at 11:59 p.m. ET on Dec. 1, this figures to be a bizarre offseason.
articles.body:
With MLB owners expected to lock the players out when the current collective bargaining agreement expires at 11:59 p.m. ET on Dec. 1, this figures to be a bizarre offseason.

What may happen is two jolts of free agency sandwiched around months of an owner-induced lockout where no action will be permitted. Given the uncertainty about whether a salary cap will return after the lockout, players might be inclined to get paid before it. Heck, there might be urgency to sign in the days and weeks before the lockout just to have certainty about where you'll live and play next season.

This isn't a free-agent class where you're going to find the face of your lineup for the next seven years. However, there are some very good complementary pieces available. Let's take a look at the top 10 hitters expected to be available in this free-agent class.

2026 Stats: .295 BA, 21 HR, 72 RBI, 37 BB, .865 OPS, 3.6 WAR

It's always difficult to know what to make of players like this heading into free agency. Between his All-Star season with the Seattle Mariners in 2022 and an excellent 2026 campaign for the Padres this year, Ty France posted a 95 OPS+ for four different teams. He was a below-average MLB player for three seasons.

At the same time, he turned 119 games this past season into the fourth-highest WAR (3.6) among qualified first basemen, with FanGraphs saying that only Pete Alonso (4.2), Willson Contreras (4.0) and Matt Olson (3.9) posted better marks than him. In addition to great offensive production, France was tremendous at first base, as evidenced by his 15 defensive runs saved and seven outs above average.

A resurgent 2026 doesn't erase 2023-2025, but it should earn France a nice multi-year free-agent deal. The two-year, $29 million deal that Ryan O'Hearn signed with the Pittsburgh Pirates last winter should be the baseline.

9. Luis Arraez: 2B, Philadelphia Phillies

2026 Stats: .310 BA, 6 HR, 64 RBI, 34 BB, .765 OPS, 4.1 WAR

Luis Arraez remains one of the most polarizing players in baseball. His 2026 campaign was not only a tale of two teams but also of two halves.

He was excellent with the San Francisco Giants, hitting .324 with a 3.8 WAR in 105 games. He wasn't the same player after getting dealt to the Phillies, batting a more modest .278 with a 0.3 WAR in 46 games before a bad left ankle sprain prevented him from suiting up in the NLWCS.

The thing with Arraez is he almost has to hit .310 to have value. The good news is he's a .316 career hitter. Because he doesn't draw many walks or hit for power, his value is pretty much exclusively tied to hitting for a high average.

Additionally, while he showed improvement at second base under the tutelage of Ron Washington this past year, defensive metrics (minus-four defensive runs saved and 12 outs above average) were divided on his work. From someone who covered the second half of his season, here's the eye test: He's passable at second base, but doesn't have the range that elite defenders at the position have.

Arraez will probably get a two-year deal, though that could feel underwhelming, considering he seemed to be trending towards a longer commitment based on how he performed from April to July.

2026 Stats: .218 BA, 24 HR, 79 RBI, 81 BB, .738 OPS, 2.6 WAR

There are old-school baseball fans who will take one look at Happ's .218 batting average and dismiss him. However, it's easier to live with a low batting average when you walk 81 times. He also hit .251 between 2022 and 2025, so you can probably expect some level of positive regression in 2027.

Additionally, Happ provides tremendous defense in the outfield. He's won four consecutive Gold Glove Awards in left field and is once again a finalist after posting 10 defensive runs saved and two outs above average in 2026.

Happ is a switch-hitter, but much better from the left side. He doesn't provide the same type of offensive ceiling as some of the other outfielders on this list, but if you like 20-25 home runs with great defense every year, you'll love Happ .

Ranking Every Player in the 2026 World Series 🔢

2026 Stats: .266 BA, 26 HR, 86 RBI, 94 BB, .874 OPS, 3.7 WAR

The only player on this list whose 2026 season isn't over is Jake Bauers. He's a major reason why, as he won NLCS MVP to help the Brewers reach the World Series for the first time since 1982.

Somewhat like France, it can be hard to know what to expect from Bauers moving forward. His .874 OPS in 2026 was tied for 10th among all qualified hitters in baseball. So far this postseason, he's got an .867 OPS. At the same time, he was a journeyman with a .672 career OPS before this season. Is Bauers a late bloomer, or is he just in the midst of a Linsanity run?

The guess here is that Bauers will get a nice two-year deal this winter, probably not from the Brewers. Then the Brewers will churn someone else completely off the radar into that spot next year and win 100-ish games.

6. Jazz Chisholm Jr.: 2B, New York Yankees

2026 Stats: .231 BA, 19 HR, 55 RBI, 56 BB, .711 OPS, 3.5 WAR

Jazz Chisholm Jr. is kind of the opposite of France and Bauers. He has a pretty long track record of being a good-to-very-good player, but he had a disappointing contract year.

Chisholm entered the year hoping to join Shohei Ohtani in the 50/50 club. While he did steal 41 bases, he wound up hitting just 19 home runs. There's a pretty strong case to be made that Chisholm is young enough that if the Yankees offer him a one-year, $23.15 million qualifying offer, he should take it and try to rebound.

If that doesn't happen, though, Chisholm could still be a candidate to get a multi-year deal in free agency. He's on the right side of 30, can slide around the diamond and is just a year removed from homering 31 times and posting an .813 OPS. A year from now, it might look like a mistake that the two-time All-Star was only at No. 6 on this list.

2026 Stats: .260 BA, 35 HR, 96 RBI, 62 BB, .824 OPS, 4.9 WAR

The Pirates weren't able to reach the postseason. They did finish with their first winning record since 2018. A major reason for that was a significant improvement in their offense, with Brandon Lowe being one of the big offseason acquisitions.

After spending the first eight seasons of his career with the Tampa Bay Rays, Lowe homered 35 times, drove in 96 runs and posted a 121 OPS+, all while playing in a career-high 150 games.

It's difficult to project how owner Bob Nutting will act, but the right move for the Pirates would be to extend the one-year, $23.15 million qualifying offer to Lowe. If he accepts it, you get a really good player for another season. If he declines it, his market could be suppressed enough that you re-sign him, or you'll get draft-pick compensation if he leaves in free agency.

Given he's 32 and has dealt with injuries before, Lowe should decline the QO if the Pirates extend him and take the best long-term deal he can get. He's not going to have a better contract year than he did in 2026.

2026 Stats: .260 BA, 18 HR, 78 RBI, 49 BB, .702 OPS, 1.9 WAR

More than anyone on this list, Bo Bichette comes with an asterisk. His first season with the Mets didn't go particularly well, so he might opt into the second year of a three-year, $126 million deal and try to set himself up for his major payday next winter.

Then again, the Phillies offered Bichette a seven-year, $200 million contract last offseason, even with a qualifying offer attached. This year, any team signing Bichette wouldn't have to give up draft-pick compensation because he's ineligible for a QO. He's still under 30 and has led the AL in hits twice. With so few impact right-handed hitters available, teams will talk themselves into Bichette if he's on the open market.

Perhaps the biggest question for Bichette will be what defensive position teams will want him to play moving forward. He has a career minus-21 defensive runs saved at his natural position of shortstop. The Mets—with Francisco Lindor at shortstop—primarily used him at third base in 2026, but he posted minus-eight DRS there. Could a team sign him with the plan to use him at second base?

2026 Stats: .306 BA, 39 HR, 106 RBI, 68 BB, .991 OPS

Based on his product in Japan, there will definitely be some who have Teruaki Sato ranked as the top offensive player available in this year's free-agent class. There are a few areas of concern, but that's hardly an outlandish opinion.

Let's start with the good: Sato has homered 79 times and driven in 208 runs over the last two seasons for the Hanshin Tigers of Nippon Professional Baseball, Japan's top league. He won't turn 28 until next March, so if he clicks stateside, he could be a long-term lineup anchor.

There are some concerns about his defensive position. Jon Heyman of The New York Post shared this scouting report of Sato's work at his natural position of third base back in July:

"Like Munetaka Murakami, who's thrived at 1B slugging for the White Sox, Sato, a former Central League MVP with a 1.026 OPS, has "good pop" but is "questionable" at 3B, via scouts."

If Sato hits like he did in Japan, the defense doesn't matter. Move him to the outfield, first base or DH. Who cares. If he's gonna hit 40 home runs and post an OPS above .800, you make it work.

In addition to questions about his defense, there are questions about how frequently he chases . Also, while his 68 walks last season are nice, you would expect a mark closer to 100 from a player with this much power (and a tendency to swing and miss).

As with many players who come over from Asian countries, there will be some variance in how teams think about the ceiling and floor for Sato. But those who like Sato will probably really like him.

2026 Stats: .270 BA, 26 HR, 86 RBI, 81 BB, .841 OPS, 4.6 WAR

Seiya Suzuki had his best MLB season yet just in time to hit the free-agent market.

It's not surprising that Suzuki continued to perform at a high offensive level, combining power production with a .368 on-base percentage. What is surprising is that Suzuki—who at times has felt more like a DH—posted 14 defensive runs saved and five outs above average across 972.2 innings in right field. By comparison, the Cubs only utilized him in right field for 282 frames in 2025. He finished with minus-four DRS and minus-one OAA.

Perspective suitors will have to decide how much they want to commit to Suzuki's best defensive season, especially since he's likely to command a four- or five-year deal. He'll also come with a qualifying offer attached. With the dearth of productive right-handed hitters in baseball right now, Suzuki is going to make out well this winter, whether it's from the Cubs or someone else.

1. Randy Arozarena: LF, Seattle Mariners

2026 Stats: .281 BA, 26 HR, 79 RBI, 68 BB, .865 OPS, 5.5 WAR

Randy Arozarena received my vote for B/R's 2026 All-MLB team as one of the top three outfielders in baseball this past regular season. He couldn't be hitting free agency at a better time.

Still, Arozarena is hardly a perfect free agent. On one hand, he just posted an .865 OPS, a remarkable accomplishment for someone who played their home games at T-Mobile Park, a spot where many hitters go to die. On the other hand, Arozarena had a much more modest .756 OPS from 2023 to 2025.

The concern with Arozarena—who is also going to receive and decline a qualifying offer—is that you would be paying for an A-level player and wind up getting B-level production. But the former ALCS MVP is a red-light player. In such a weak market, he figures he'll get over $100 million.

articles.title: Latest MLB Free Agents 2026 Rumors, Predictions Amid World Series
articles.summary: The Tampa Bay Rays will look to notch their first victory of the 2026 World Series Monday night at Tropicana Field when they host Game 3 against the Milwaukee Brewers.
articles.body:
The Tampa Bay Rays will look to notch their first victory of the 2026 World Series Monday night at Tropicana Field when they host Game 3 against the Milwaukee Brewers.

For those teams not involved in this year's Fall Classic, their attention is on the offseason and the free agents they can acquire to help bolster their rosters and ensure they are not watching from the sidelines next October.

What is the latest, and where might some of the prized free agents end up?

Potential Landing Spots for Tarik Skubal

The prized free agent from this year's class is undeniably two-time Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal.

Fresh off an early elimination from the postseason with the Los Angeles Dodgers, the lefty will likely sign a historic deal this offseason, but the question remains: "with who?"

MLB.com's Mark Feinsand named the incumbent Dodgers, his former squad, the Detroit Tigers, the New York Mets, the Chicago Cubs, the Toronto Blue Jays, and the Philadelphia Phillies as potential landing spots for the game's best pitcher.

"Obviously, he's the best and most accomplished starting pitcher to hit free agency in a number of years. I think the main thing to keep an eye out for is the timing of his signing; I think labor uncertainty could stop big market teams from pursuing him with the same vigor as someone like [Juan] Soto, but the big question is whether or not Dec. 1 will be a deadline for him."

It may take longer to get him under contract, and any potential labor dispute may throw a wrench in any team's desire to get him in the building sooner, but there is no doubt that any contending team looking for an ace will be contacting Scott Boras about his client.

With that said, with big money expected, the two teams that make the most sense are the Dodgers and the Mets.

If Los Angeles can do enough to prove to Skubal that this year was an anomaly and that the team is not the aging unit it looked like at times in the playoffs, one would have to figure they would be the front runner.

The Mets, though, are a young team with pieces in Carson Benge, AJ Ewing, and Nolan McLean that have them set up nicely for the future. Add in future Hall of Famers Juan Soto and Francisco Lindor and you have a team that, with the right coaching, is a World Series contender.

Even more so with Skubal in the rotation.

One team's window appears to be potentially closing while another is just opening. That could be the difference between the West and East Coast for Skubal.

It was a mixed bag for Bichette in his first season with the New York Mets and, with an opt-out clause in play, it may prove to be his lone season in the Big Apple.

The former Blue Jay came on strong after the break and ended the season hitting .260, with 18 home runs, 78 RBI, and 49 walks, showing improved plate discipline.

That, coupled with the aforementioned flashes of future brilliance in the young players in the Mets lineup, and the uncertainty of the labor dispute, suggests Queens may be the perfect place for the shortstop/third baseman to continue his career.

That he positively discussed his time in New York this past August with Mike Puma of the New York Post, stating, "I am having a really good time here right now. There are a lot of really good young players that make it fun to come here and a lot of really good players that have been around, so I am enjoying my time here," only heightens reasons to believe he would return.

He could return to Toronto, where his affect on the lineup was obvious, or he could move on to NL East rival Philadelphia.

His case is, perhaps, the most uncertain of all, but it feels like he has unfinished business in New York.

Prediction: Bichette opts in, stays with the Mets

Does Freddy Peralta Return to Tampa Bay?

The Tampa Bay righty achieved ALCS MVP honors for his play against the Cleveland Guardians. He has also been one of the best pitchers in the game since August, with a sub-1.0 ERA and the sort of fastball dominance that was missing during his brief and disastrous stint with the Mets.

If he sustains his level of play through his start Monday night in Tampa, and can finish the season strong, one would have to assume the Rays would make a play to keep him on the mound.

Tampa, though, is not necessarily known for paying big-money price tags for free agents. They carry one of the lowest payrolls in baseball and forking over tens of millions for Peralta, who should command a sizeable payday considering his work for the team, may be out of the question.

Maybe he stays and chases another World Series appearance with a team that should remain mostly intact, but that will likely be on Peralta and his willingness to take a pay cut.

Prediction: Peralta leaves and signs elsewhere

articles.title: Yankees Birthday of the Day: Snuffy Stirnweiss
articles.summary: The man known as “Snuffy” had two of the best individual seasons in Yankees’ history.
articles.body:
According to Baseball Reference WAR, Babe Ruth, Lou Gehrig, Mickey Mantle, Aaron Judge, Rickey Henderson, Alex Rodriguez, and Joe DiMaggio are the only Yankees position players to have had better single seasons in pinstripes than George "Snuffy" Stirnweiss. All of those guys are either Hall of Famers, on the road to be (Judge), or have the stats to be and aren't in because of…reasons (A-Rod). As for Stirnweiss, his greatness came in part due to circumstances beyond any baseball player's control.

However, his 1944 and '45 seasons are forever in the record books as some of the best in franchise history. On what would have been his 108th birthday, let's look back on the life and times of "Snuffy."

George Henry "Snuffy" Stirnweiss Born: October 26, 1918 (New York, NY) Died: September 15, 1958 (Newark Bay, NJ) Yankees Tenure: 1943-50

George Stirnweiss was born to Andy and Sophie in 1918 in the city he would later play professionally in: New York. He showed an aptitude for athletics from a very early age, starring for Fordham Prep in baseball, football, and basketball. Back then, football was the sport he was arguably best at, and he parlayed that success into a college sports career at the University of North Carolina.

While at UNC, he would captain both the football and baseball teams, the gridiron was primarily where he generated headlines. He did a little bit of everything for the Tar Heels, playing a quarterback/running back hybrid position. (Football was way different in the 1930s.) Besides that, he also punted and returned punts, playing all over the field.

During that time, he was also starring on the baseball field, hitting .390 as a senior. That caught the eye of legendary Yankees' scout Paul Krichell. While Stirnweiss was selected by the then Chicago Cardinals in the second round of the 1940 NFL draft, Krichell and baseball won Stirnweiss over, as he thought the diamond provided him better professional future than the gridiron. Upon his graduation, he inked a deal with the Yankees, who had been his childhood favorite team.

Stirnweiss started his career with the Norfolk Tars of the Piedmondt League. There he got his "Snuffy" nickname. A teammate dubbed him "Snuffy" after seeing Stirnweiss use both chewing tobacco and a cigar, asking Stirnweiss where the snuff was as well.

After a couple good years in the minors, Stirnweiss impressed manager Joe McCarthy in spring training 1943. Impressed by his speed and potential, McCarthy took a liking to him and named him to the team's roster despite the fact that his preferred second base position was occupied by Joe Gordon.

Stirnweiss made his MLB debut on Opening Day of 1943, playing shortstop and hitting leadoff. He recorded his first hit with an RBI single off Early Wynn of the Washington Senators in the fifth inning in a 5-4 win. While he did get the start in a prominent spot in his first big league game, Stirnweiss ended up more in a utility role in the 1943 season. He appeared in 83 games, hitting .219/.333/.288 (82 OPS+), playing mostly at shortstop with Phil Rizzuto away in the military.

That year, Stirnweiss also helped the Yankees to the AL Pennant and a World Series matchup against the Cardinals. He played in just one game and got one plate appearance in the Fall Classic, but it ended up being a bit of an important one. With a runner on first, He laid down a sacrifice bunt attempt with the Yankees down 2-1 in the eighth inning of Game 3. Cardinals' third baseman Whitey Kurowski made an error on the play, allowing all runners to be safe. The Yankees ended up scoring five runs in the frame, as they took a 2-1 lead in the series, which they eventually won in five games.

Gordon was drafted into the military ahead of 1944, and Stirnweiss became the regular second baseman and turned in two of the most underrated great seasons in Yankees' history. In that first season, he led the league in hits (205), triples (16), and stolen bases (55). He finished just a couple points off the batting title and put up, in retrospect, a 139 OPS+ and an AL position player-leading 8.6 rWAR and a 9.0 fWAR. With several other prominent Yankees away, he was the team's best player. Unfortunately for him and the team, without the players that were away serving, the Yankees fell to third in the AL. Despite all that, Stirnweiss finished fourth in MVP voting, and arguably could've won.

So, how do you follow up a historic breakout season? If you're Stirnweiss, you put up an even better one. In 1945, Stirnweiss led the league in hits, runs, triples, stolen bases, batting average, slugging percentage, total bases, rWAR, and fWAR. The most eventful of those leaderboards was the batting title race, which went right down to the last game of the season.

On the final day of 1945, Tony Cuccinello of the White Sox went into the day at .308, leading Stirnweiss, .306, by just a couple points. On that day, Chicago saw their game rained out and wasn't required to be finished. Meanwhile, over in New York, the Yankees played their game. Stirnweiss made the most of things, going 3-for-5. His batting average rounded up just enough to finish at .309, giving him the batting title by just a single point. Historically, that wasn't a particularly high BA to win the title, but Stirnweiss is forever one of a handful of Yankees to have accomplished that feat.

Admittedly, the league as a whole was weakened by players away in the military, and Stirnweiss never reached those peaks again. He still remained a regular for the Yankees for the next several years, helping them to championships in 1947 and '49.

By the end of his Yankee career, Stirnweiss had been overtaken at second base by Jerry Coleman. That led to him being traded to the St. Louis Browns in June 1950. He was traded to Cleveland after that season and spent parts of the next two seasons there. Stirnweiss didn't return to the majors after 1952 but spent a couple years after that playing and managing in the minors. He eventually left baseball to get more stable work.

In 1958, Stirnweiss was working as a foreign freight agent when on September 15th, while on his way to work, he died when the train he was on derailed and slid into Newark Bay. Stirnweiss was sadly one of 48 people who lost their lives in the accident, passing away a month short of his 40th birthday.

In addition to tragically leaving behind a wife and six children, Stirnweiss' death also left his former teammates devastated — especially Rizzuto. The Scooter credited Stirnweiss with helping him eventually land the Yankee broadcaster job, which made him a beloved figure for generations. After the Yankees released Rizzuto as a player, he was irate. Stirnweiss told him to go home and cool down before he did anything he regretted. Rizzuto did so, avoiding harsh public critique of team management or ownership, which might have ended his broadcasting gig before it ever even came about.

Stirnweiss wasn't good enough long enough to get a place in Monument Park or his number retired or anything like that. However, there are few players who has as good a two-year run as he did.

articles.title: MLB Rule Changes to Promote Offense Revealed for Experiments During Fall League
articles.summary: MLB is reportedly exploring ways to increase offensive production with some new rules for the Arizona Fall League.
articles.body:
MLB is reportedly exploring ways to increase offensive production with some new rules for the Arizona Fall League.

Per David Brandt of the Associated Press, the league is experimenting with "restricting the positioning of outfielders on every at-bat."

"The idea is that making outfielders play straight up — instead of adjusting for individual hitters' tendencies — will lead to more doubles and triples," Brandt explained.

Brandt noted that infielders "also have new positioning requirements when there are no runners on base, limiting how much they can shift for a hitter's tendencies."

The 2026 postseason has highlighted the lack of offensive production, as pitchers have been able to dominate from the mound. According to Brandt, teams have combined for a .216 batting average through 37 playoff games this year. New rules that debuted in 2023, like the pitch clock, did little to improve offensive numbers.

"Game times are about 25 minutes shorter and stolen bases are up, but batting average (.243 in 2022 and .244 in 2026), runs per game (4.28 in 2022, 4.48 in 2026) and hits per game (8.16 in 2022, 8.20 in 2026) haven't changed much," Brandt explained.

The Arizona Fall League has become MLB's hub for testing potential rule changes. The AFL had experimented with the Automated Ball-Strike system long before it debuted in the majors this year. Brandt noted that MLB "declined official comment on the most recent experiment, and any change to big-league rules would still be years away."

MLB's attempts to move the game forward have yet to pay off, but this latest idea could help to achieve the goal of raising offensive statistics.

articles.title: MLB testing restrictions on outfielder positioning in Arizona Fall League, hoping to boost extra-base hits
articles.summary: Under the new rule, outfielders have to play 'straight up,' rather than shifting in one direction or another based on an opposing hitter's tendencies.
articles.body:
Major League Baseball saw a slight uptick in the amount of runs per game this season, with 4.48 scored. However, the league apparently wants to see more offense — or at least more action on the bases with more doubles and triples in game action.

In an effort to boost that activity, MLB is testing a new rule that would require outfielders to play their positions "straight up," rather than shifting in one direction or another to defend against an opposing hitter's tendencies, according to the Associated Press .

The new rule is being tested in the Arizona Fall League, which began on Oct. 3 and news of the restrictions was reported then . Outfielders will be shown whether or not they're positioned correctly by a small video board. If they're playing straight up, a green "O" will be shown for their position. Anyone shading to the left or right, playing more shallow or deep, will see a red "X" telling them to move.

However, the new rule only applies to games being played at Salt River Fields, the spring training home of the Arizona Diamondbacks and Colorado Rockies, because the ballpark has technology similar to what's utilized at MLB stadiums.

"We talked to our guys about embracing it, it only happens in our ballpark, so embrace it and move on," Salt River Rafters manager Ted Tom told the AP . "There's going to be some things that we've never seen before. That's OK, just keep playing."

"The hardest part is cutting off doubles in the gap and they're even turning into triples," Minnesota Twins prospect Kyle DeBarge told the AP's David Brandt . "That's what they told us they wanted in the beginning. So it works."

Though the outfield restrictions are designed to potentially increase offense, the possibility of creating more impressive defensive plays — such as an outfielder running and diving into the gap, or running back to the wall — could increase, as well.

Thus far, one casualty in game play has been bloop singles because the restrictions force outfielders to play more shallow.

"Your first move is always back with how shallow you are — lots of running, said Teo Banks, a Washington Nationals prospect. "But I think there's some part of strategy that's taken away with something like this."

Asked if the new rule might be too drastic of a change, Tom smiled and didn't answer the question.

The Arizona Fall League has already been a testing ground for rules that were later implemented in the minor leagues and then the majors, such as the pitch clock and prohibiting infield shifts.

While those changes have helped increase pace and reduce the length of games, they have had little effect on offense.

The numbers of runs and hits per game have only upticked slightly in the past 15 years or so , while doubles and triples have roughly stayed the same. Batting average has decreased during the past 10 years (though harder-throwing pitchers and more strikeouts is more responsible for that).

articles.title: Alex Cora Addresses His MLB Managerial Future After Red Sox Firing, Phillies Rumors
articles.summary: After reportedly turning down two offers to become the manager of the Philadelphia Phillies, former Boston Red Sox manager Alex Cora is still open to returning to the dugout in 2027.
articles.body:
After reportedly turning down two offers to become the manager of the Philadelphia Phillies, former Boston Red Sox manager Alex Cora is still open to returning to the dugout in 2027.

Cora, who was fired by the Red Sox in April after a 10-17 start, told Rob Bradford on the Baseball isn't Boring podcast that he won't rule out a return to managing, but he won't officially commit to coming back next year.

"I don't know, man. We have to wait and see. We've still got one more year for that, which is great," Cora said, noting he's still getting paid by Boston through next season, per Justin Tasch of the New York Post . "If we decide as a family that's the route we want to take, we'll do it. It'd be cool to go through the process again, it'd be cool. It will help whoever — if I decide I want to go through the process and somebody gives us a chance to interview, it'd be good for them to hear it, how I see it, my values as a manager, understand everything that goes with it and go from there, and they make a decision."

He went on to add: "I'm not 100 percent sure I want to do it."

Tasch noted that Phillies president of baseball operations Dave Dombrowski, who had previously worked with Cora in Boston, offered him the managerial opening during the 2026 season, but Cora turned it down to spend time with his family. He turned down the job again after the 2026 campaign, and Philadelphia elevated interim manager Don Mattingly to the full-time position.

Cora told Bradford that he still talks to Dombrowski frequently, and he was one of the first people he spoke to after being fired in April.

"I've got to be very honest — obviously pride comes into play early on, but then when people that you really care (about) and you love, they fly into Boston and they slow things down, it's like, OK, we've got to make sure we do the right thing," Cora said of talking with Dombrowski in the aftermath of the firing. "You have to make sure you take care of your people. And I think the best thing for the Cora-Felicianos is this, is to stay away and, at that point, kind of regroup and enjoy."

Cora led the Red Sox to a World Series title in 2018, so he will surely draw interest if he chooses to return to managing. For now, it sounds like he's content to take a wait-and-see approach before committing to a comeback.

articles.title: World Series 2026: Former big leaguer Daniel Vogelbach is bringing energy and game-planning as hitting coach for Brewers' high-flying offense
