articles.body:
ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — The Milwaukee Brewers have made a habit of turning early deficits into riveting comeback victories en route to a 2-0 lead over the Tampa Bay Rays in the World Series, and there's plenty of reasons behind their ability to do so.

It starts with the personnel, a lineup featuring a healthy balance of star-level sluggers and deft role players all capable of delivering a big swing or executing whatever less-glamorous job the game situation requires. There's manager Pat Murphy, who has instilled a mentality of relentlessness that is apparent in how the hitters approach every plate appearance. That messaging is maximized by the continuity on Murphy's staff, with several coaches who honed their teaching skills in the Brewers organization for years before matriculating to the major-league level.

But if you've watched Milwaukee this season, you might have noticed another key cog in its offensive infrastructure, someone you might recognize from his playing days. You can often see him getting fired up on the top step of the dugout or reviewing scouting reports with hitters during a pitching change. And if you're one of those Brewers hitters tasked with conjuring a late rally, there's no doubt you can hear him as well.

Said rookie shortstop Cooper Pratt: "He has that energy where we'll be down like 2-0 in the ninth or 5-0, and it'll kind of be silent, and you'll just hear him screaming in the dugout. After every inning, especially when [the opponents] score runs, we'll come in, and you just hear Vogey screaming, like, 'Let's put it on these guys!'"

Pratt is referring to Daniel Vogelbach, who played parts of nine major-league seasons from 2016 to 2024 before making a pivot to coaching. After spending 2025 with the Pirates as a special assistant to the hitting department, Vogelbach jumped at the opportunity to join Murphy's staff ahead of the 2026 season.

"I knew I wanted to coach. I didn't know I wanted to do it this fast," Vogelbach said.

"Murph called, and it's hard to say no to this organization and Murph with everything they have."

Vogelbach was drafted by the Cubs out of a Florida high school in 2011, then was traded to the Mariners as a minor leaguer in the deal that netted Chicago left-hander Mike Montgomery, who went on to record the final out of the 2016 World Series. Vogelbach's peak performance as a major leaguer came when he hit 30 homers and was named an All-Star with Seattle in 2019, but it was his stint with the Brewers in 2021 that left a lasting impression.

"When I played here, [Murph] wasn't managing. He was a bench coach," Vogelbach recalled. "But he made an impact on me. And we stayed in contact ever since I left here. And whether I went back and coached or didn't coach, I feel like I could call Murph a friend forever."

Vogelbach played three more seasons with the Pirates, Mets and Blue Jays before his playing career concluded. But his experience with the Brewers stuck with him, making it an easy decision when the opportunity to reunite with Murphy arose.

"You look at the group of people here — and I played with some of them — but just the way they play the game and their personalities, you want to be a part of it," Vogelbach said.

"He connects with people," Murphy said of the guy they call Vogey. "He has the ability to tell the truth. He has the ability to be loving and bestow discipline on how you approach a pitcher. He's great with information. He's great working together with people. He's fun. He's the same every day. He's high-end intensity. He's real."

Said third-base coach Matt Erickson: "There was always a mutual respect between our staff and [Vogelbach]. And I know Murph was a big fan of him, and so when we had the opportunity to bring him over and be a part of our hitting team, it was a no-brainer."

As a player, Vogelbach was a distinctly disciplined left-handed hitter. His physical presence always conveyed power as his calling card — and he did hit some titanic home runs — but it was Vogelbach's keen approach that separated him from his peers, as he regularly registered among the lowest chase rates and highest walk rates in the league. Those foundational skills, borne out of preparation and studying opposing pitchers, have carried over into his routines and messaging as a hitting coach.

"What you see is what you get from Vogey," president of baseball operations Matt Arnold said. "It's high-energy and ready to compete and quality at-bats. That's what he preaches all the time, and he helps establish the standards that Murph talks about all the time and does a fantastic job."

Said first baseman Jake Bauers : "Vogey's been big for us as a team this year, and I know for sure he's played a big role in my own approach at the plate."

"The guy works his ass off," Bauers added. "If you ever catch him at the team hotel, he's going to be sitting in the lobby in the morning, drinking two full cold brews and watching video. He's been big in developing approaches not only for starters but in the dugout, just giving you some quick tips on what to look for, where to look for and stuff like that."

Not swinging at pitches outside the strike zone has been a fundamental part of Bauers' late-career breakout and the Milwaukee lineup's collective success: In 2026, the Brewers swung at 29.1% of pitches outside the zone, the lowest mark in MLB . It's hardly a revolutionary concept, but it's a tenet of hitting that can be difficult to put into practice against the best pitchers in the world. That said, it helps to be prepared.

"I do think that in this game, it is really hard to hit for a long period of time if you don't have a plan," Vogelbach said. "I think there are certain hitters that can do it because they're so talented. But the pitching is so good now, and they throw so hard and make the ball go so many different ways that I do think you have to have a plan and be really stubborn to that plan."

Before Vogelbach's arrival, Milwaukee already had a strong hitting infrastructure in place. Lead hitting coach Eric Theisen is in his second season on the major-league staff after spending four years coaching in the minors with Milwaukee. Former major leaguer Jason Lane — promoted to offense and strategy coordinator in January, when Vogelbach joined the hitting group alongside another new voice in Guillermo Martinez — in his 11th season on Milwaukee's staff.

"He's built upon it," designated hitter Andrew Vaughn said. "I remember getting here last year, that was Murph's big thing: 'What we do here is we swing at strikes, and we take balls.' As simple as that. And being able to fine-tune that and understanding pitchers and what they're trying to do to you — Vogey really breaks that down and gives us a set plan."

Added third-base coach Erickson: "I think we got a lot of people in the right spots right now. And [Vogelbach] fits in perfectly."

Vogelbach does not take this opportunity lightly.

"I like to take it the same way I was playing," he said. "It's just when the game starts, I'm in the dugout, and I'm not on the field. I think in this game and any professional sport, if you don't give it your all and you don't fully commit to it, you probably shouldn't be a part of it."

"When you're playing, you have a job to do that isn't just on the field — it's preparing, giving yourself a best chance to perform that night," he continued. "So when you're coaching, it's the same thing. You have to get these guys ready to play and do everything you can. If you're not, you're not doing your job."

As the World Series shifts to Florida , Vogelbach is focused on his small but integral part in the run-scoring machine that has helped push Milwaukee to the precipice of its first World Series title. And his experience on Murphy's staff has only further stoked his ambitions as he navigates his post-playing career.

"Managing is what I want to do," Vogelbach said. "I want to lead a group of people. I think that's the coolest thing. Murph talks about it all the time — I think impacting human beings is the greatest thing in the world. Whether you're in sports or whether you're not, I think impacting people and leading a group is special."

Murphy, the two-time NL Manager of the Year with a strong chance to win the award again next month, can envision that for the newest member of his staff.

"He's got a real future in this game, and I don't think it's as a hitting coach," he said. "I think he can lead."

articles.title: Watch Francisco Lindor's Emotional Reaction in Video as Mets Star Wins Roberto Clemente Award
articles.summary: Francisco Lindor received a prestigious honor on Monday as the New York Mets shortstop was given the Roberto Clemente Award for his work in the community.
articles.body:
Francisco Lindor received a prestigious honor on Monday as the New York Mets shortstop was given the Roberto Clemente Award for his work in the community.

The award meant everything to Lindor and his wife, Katia.

"This is something when our kids grow up, they're gonna look back and say my mom and dad were very cool because they were blessing others and helping others," he said.

The Clemente Award is given annually to the player who "best represents the game of baseball through extraordinary character, community involvement, philanthropy and positive contributions on and off the field," making it one of the highest off-the-field honors.

Lindor has been the Mets' nominee for the Clemente Award in each of the last four seasons and is the first member of the organization to win it since Curtis Granderson in 2016.

Lindor has donated more than $1 million since 2020 to build a two-story middle school building at his alma mater, Montverde Academy in Florida. He also established his own scholarship fund for students who wouldn't otherwise be able to attend the school.

Lindor provided financial support and helped restore athletic facilities in his hometown of Caguas, Puerto Rico, after Hurricane Maria in 2017 and Fiona in 2022.

His "Lindor's Leaders" development program launched this year for students in Bayside High School's Sports Medicine Program, and he partnered with Seen, a nonprofit helping families with children with physical disabilities.

"Sometimes, us athletes can be seen like we're so far away from the general public," Lindor said . "But we're not. We are in the communities. We are giving back. We are helping. Hopefully, this is going to give me a bigger platform to continue to help."

Lindor has already had an outstanding career that features five All-Star nods, a Gold Glove Award and four Silver Slugger Awards, and now he's added one of the highest honors in sports to his resume.

"It's a little bit surreal, you know?" Lindor said. "It's bigger than baseball, in a way. Like, we are in the entertainment business, and we are there to bring smiles and joy to people, but also to carry it off the field to me is even cooler. So it's something that I'll forever continue to do."

articles.title: Game 1 of Rays-Brewers World Series sees slight step back in ratings from 2024 and '25
articles.summary: Besides the recent pair of World Series featuring the Dodgers, this was the most-watched Fall Classic Game 1 since 2019.
articles.body:
The small-market World Series did nearly as well ratings-wise as the recent pair of big-market World Series in Game 1.

Game 1 of the 2026 Fall Classic between the Milwaukee Brewers and Tampa Bay Rays drew a combined average of 12.2 million viewers on Fox and Univision, according to preliminary numbers acquired by Sports Business Journal's Austin Karp . The game reportedly peaked at 13 million.

The final number will be available Tuesday afternoon.

For now, the 12.2 million number is a step back from the recent pair of World Series featuring the Los Angeles Dodgers, as Game 1 in 2024 against the New York Yankees drew 15.2 million and Game 1 in 2025 against the Toronto Blue Jays drew 13.3 million.

That said, 12.2 million is still above some doom-and-gloom expectations brought on by a Fall Classic between teams in two of MLB's smallest markets. Excepting the past two World Series, it's the best number since the ratings collapse brought on by the COVID-19 pandemic. By comparison, Game 1 of the 2023 World Series between the Texas Rangers and Arizona Diamondbacks drew a record-low 9.4 million.

There had been a bogus 15.2 million number floating around on social media Saturday that appeared to be brought on by an AI hallucination drawing from a Sports Media Watch comment section .

Game 1 of this World Series saw the Brewers take a 1-0 lead over the Rays via a strong pitching performance from Jacob Misiorowski and the bullpen . That lead has since expanded to 2-0 with a four-run Brewers comeback on Saturday .

articles.title: Mets Promote Minor League Coach to MLB Staff
articles.summary: The New York Mets are promoting Mariano Duncan to their major league coaching staff, the New York Post’s Joel Sherman reported Monday. Sherman says that Dunc...
articles.body:
The New York Mets are promoting Mariano Duncan to their major league coaching staff, the New York Post's Joel Sherman reported Monday. Sherman says that Duncan is "expected to assist in multiple areas with the position player group."

Mets Promote Minor League Coach Mariano Duncan to MLB Staff

Duncan, 63, is set to enter his ninth season with the organization. He joined the Mets in 2019, serving on the Kingsport coaching staff before becoming High-A Brooklyn's bench coach in 2021. He spent the past five seasons as Double-A Binghamton's bench coach, helping the Rumble Ponies win the Eastern League championship in 2025.

Earlier this month, the Mets, who have openings for their coaching staff, interviewed long-time hitting coach Kevin Long and have shown interest in interviewing hitting coach John Mallee for a role on the staff. On Monday, however, Long and the Mets reportedly did not "match and he is no longer a consideration." As for Mallee, he too has reportedly withdrawn his name from a coaching role consideration with New York.

Duncan brings extensive familiarity with the Mets' player development system, having worked with prospects moving through the organization . His background also includes major league coaching experience, serving as the Los Angeles Dodgers' first-base coach from 2006–10.

Before working for the Mets, Duncan worked as a minor league hitting instructor in the Dodgers, Chicago Cubs and Detroit Tigers organizations. A former MLB infielder, Duncan played 12 seasons with the Dodgers, Cincinnati Reds, Philadelphia Phillies, New York Yankees and Toronto Blue Jays. He won World Series championships with Cincinnati in 1990 and New York in 1996, earning an All-Star selection with Philadelphia in 1994.

Duncan's promotion gives manager Andy Green 's staff a coach whose experience spans both major league dugouts and the daily work of developing prospects. After years spent working with players throughout the organization, he will now help the position player group at the highest level. His exact responsibilities remain unclear, but his background in hitting instruction and five seasons with the organization's minor league staff give him several areas of experience to draw upon in his new role.
